strengths: Significance: Integrating second-scale event detection with overnight representations addresses a useful clinical modeling problem. Pretraining on 20,964 PSG recordings across several cohorts is substantial, and evaluation covers staging, breathing-event segmentation, disease prediction, and adaptation.

Empirical merits: Table 2 reports strong SDB segmentation macro-F1 improvements over the evaluated baselines on both SHHS1 and KISS. Table 1 also shows improved SHHS1 staging accuracy and macro-F1. These results support the usefulness of the learned local representations.

Originality: Combining private/shared multimodal encoders with a demographic-guided, bidirectional sequence encoder is a plausible methodological contribution. Table 4 provides encouraging evidence that adding the Macro-Encoder improves staging and AHI estimation beyond the Micro-Encoder alone.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture diagrams are informative, and the appendices provide dataset descriptions, channel specifications, architecture dimensions, and training hyperparameters. The manuscript candidly acknowledges weaker KISS staging performance and possible hardware sensitivity. Appendix A.4 describes IRB approval and de-identification for KVSS.
weaknesses: Soundness—participant separation is unresolved. Appendix A.2 states that the entire eligible SHHS2 dataset is used for pretraining while SHHS1 is partitioned for downstream evaluation. Since SHHS2 is a follow-up visit from the same cohort, this protocol can expose the model to later recordings from SHHS1 test participants. The paper does not document participant-level exclusion across visits. This is particularly consequential for prospective disease prediction. An overlap audit and participant-disjoint evaluation are needed before the SHHS generalization claims are reliable.

Soundness—the central macrostructure claim is insufficiently isolated. DGCL directly encourages demographic similarity; demographic clustering in Figure 6 and improved age/sex prediction therefore do not establish learning of sleep cycles or temporal architecture. Table 4 changes both the architecture and training objective, while Tables 11–12 do not compare DGCL against demographic regression, temporal pooling, or an otherwise identical sequence encoder trained with another objective. Temporal-order controls and direct macrostructure measurements would distinguish sequence understanding from demographic shortcuts. Fixed 90-minute windows also do not establish alignment with individual sleep cycles.

Disease prediction lacks essential validation details. Table 3 provides no event counts, follow-up distributions, confidence intervals, or clear handling of prevalent disease and censoring. There is no demographic-only baseline, despite explicitly training representations to encode major cardiovascular risk factors. Table 10 specifies batches of four subjects for Cox training without explaining whether risk sets span the cohort or only each batch. These omissions prevent assessment of the survival objective and the claimed clinical value beyond demographics.

Evaluation breadth and uncertainty do not support the broad superiority claims. On KISS staging, SleepMaMi trails MOMENT substantially: 62.8% versus 69.8% accuracy and 60.6 versus 66.3 macro-F1. KISS already contributes 6,064 pretraining recordings, so its result is not a clean unseen-hardware test. Disease results are mixed, and the external ISRUC experiment compares only against SleepFM on 18 test subjects. Repeated few-shot selections, subject-level uncertainty estimates, and clearer baseline checkpoint, feature-extraction, and tuning protocols are needed.

Reproducibility and numerical reporting have material gaps. The manuscript does not provide code/checkpoint availability or sufficiently specify variable-channel handling, embedding pooling, and construction of the linear probes. The preprocessing description places 60 Hz filtering after resampling to 100 Hz, requiring clarification. Figure 11's SHHS1 staging confusion matrix yields pooled Cohen's kappa of approximately 0.743, whereas Table 1 reports 0.700; its accuracy and macro-F1 do match the table. Any different aggregation convention should be stated.

Limitations and ethics need treatment specific to demographic supervision. Calling demographic attributes 'noise-free ground truth' for sleep architecture overstates their role: they are proxy supervision and can encode cohort or acquisition differences. Although hardware sensitivity is acknowledged, the paper does not assess subgroup performance or whether demographic alignment suppresses clinically important variation within demographic groups. These are relevant unresolved limitations of the proposed objective, particularly given the claims of universal and reliable clinical applicability.

strengths: Significance: Learning reusable PSG representations across sleep staging, respiratory-event segmentation, and disease prediction is a useful research goal. Pretraining on 20,964 recordings from multiple cohorts provides a substantial empirical foundation.

Originality: The combination of private/shared micro-encoders, reconstruction and contrastive objectives, and a demographic-guided bidirectional macro-encoder is a potentially useful integration. Demographic similarity offers an interesting source of supervision that avoids dependence on manually scored sleep stages.

Empirical merits: SleepMaMi achieves the highest reported SHHS1 staging macro-F1 (74.1%) and SDB segmentation macro-F1 on both datasets (60.6% and 75.4%). Table 4 reports improvements from adding the macro-encoder, including staging accuracy from 79.8% to 81.9% and AHI MAE from 9.69 to 8.40.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture diagrams and appendix provide useful dataset, architecture, and optimization details. The authors explicitly acknowledge the weaker KISS staging results and possible hardware sensitivity; this candid discussion is valuable.
weaknesses: Soundness—subject separation is unresolved. Appendix A.2 states that the entire SHHS2 dataset is used for pretraining, while SHHS1 is partitioned for downstream evaluation. SHHS2 contains follow-up visits from SHHS1 participants, but the manuscript does not describe excluding SHHS1 validation/test participants from SHHS2 pretraining. This creates a material risk of participant overlap, including demographic supervision on evaluation subjects. A participant-level overlap audit and, if necessary, clean retraining are needed before interpreting SHHS1 results as generalization to unseen subjects.

Soundness—the central macrostructure interpretation is not established. Demographic clustering and improved age/sex prediction largely demonstrate recovery of the pretraining targets. Staging and AHI gains are encouraging, but Table 4 changes both architecture and training objective. There are no matched temporal-encoder controls, shuffled-order experiments, or direct evaluations of cycle structure and fragmentation. Demographic similarity also need not imply similar individual sleep architecture, and fixed 90-minute windows are not measured sleep cycles. The current evidence supports useful demographic supervision more clearly than learning the claimed global sleep structure.

Disease-prediction evidence is insufficient for the clinical claims. Table 3 omits event counts, confidence intervals, detailed endpoint/censoring definitions, and demographic-only risk baselines. Because pretraining explicitly emphasizes age, sex, and BMI, comparison against these established risk predictors is essential to establish additional value from PSG. Appendix C specifies a Cox-loss batch size of four subjects without explaining whether risk sets span the full training population or only each minibatch. This leaves the implementation of Equation 7 unclear.

Evaluation does not justify broad superiority or robustness claims. MOMENT substantially outperforms SleepMaMi on KISS staging: 69.8% versus 62.8% accuracy and 66.3% versus 60.6% macro-F1. Disease results are mixed. The hardware explanation remains speculative, especially because 6,064 KISS recordings already enter pretraining. Baseline checkpoint selection, temporal context, feature extraction, and tuning are insufficiently specified to establish comparable probing conditions. The unseen-dataset few-shot experiment compares only against SleepFM and lacks repeated subject sampling or uncertainty estimates.

Originality and attribution remain incompletely supported. Most architectural and loss ingredients are established, so the contribution depends on demonstrating the benefit of their specific combination. Table 11 provides useful cumulative staging ablations, but does not isolate MoE, representation negatives, or the macro-encoder objective against credible alternatives. The claimed explanation that MAE drives respiratory segmentation gains is not tested with segmentation ablations. The assertion of being the first model to encode both temporal scales also needs a more precise comparison with existing sleep foundation models.

Reproducibility and presentation contain material ambiguities. Section 3.3 describes resampling to 100 Hz before applying a 60 Hz ECG cutoff and 60 Hz notch filter, which exceed the resulting Nyquist frequency; the actual operation order must be clarified. Figure 11's SHHS1 staging confusion matrix yields approximately 74.3% pooled kappa, whereas Table 1 reports 70.0%, despite matching accuracy and macro-F1. If a different aggregation explains this, it should be stated. No code/checkpoint availability statement is provided.

Limitations and research ethics need treatment proportionate to the clinical framing. Appendix A.4 documents IRB approval and de-identification for KVSS, and I see no demonstrated ethical violation. However, demographic-guided learning is not evaluated for subgroup disparities or demographic shortcuts. Calling demographic metadata 'noise-free ground truth' overstates its relationship to sleep physiology. The unsupported suggestion of reliable clinical application should be narrowed pending calibration, subgroup evaluation, and stronger external validation.

strengths: Significance: Integrating short-duration physiological events with full-night context addresses a useful clinical modeling problem. Pretraining on 20,964 recordings and evaluating staging, breathing-event segmentation, disease prediction, and adaptation gives the work meaningful breadth.

Empirical strengths: Breathing-event segmentation is the most convincing result. Table 2 reports macro-F1 of 60.6 on SHHS1 and 75.4 on KISS, exceeding the strongest listed baselines by 11.8 points on both datasets. SHHS1 sleep-staging macro-F1 also improves substantially.

Originality: Demographic-guided contrastive learning offers an interesting approach to learning overnight representations without manually scored sleep labels. Combining this objective with a hierarchical multimodal encoder is a potentially useful contribution, although its proposed mechanism needs stronger validation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture diagrams are clear, and the appendices provide substantial dataset, architecture, optimization, ablation, and confusion-matrix details. The discussion candidly acknowledges the weaker KISS staging performance and possible hardware sensitivity.
weaknesses: Soundness—participant separation is unresolved. Appendix A.2 explicitly uses the entire SHHS2 cohort for pretraining while evaluating held-out SHHS1 participants. Because SHHS2 is a follow-up visit from the same study, this protocol permits pretraining on later recordings of evaluation participants unless participant-level exclusions were applied. No such exclusions or overlap audit are reported. This threatens the independence of the central SHHS1 results and particularly complicates prospective disease prediction. An identity-disjoint evaluation across visits is needed.

Soundness—the central macro-structure claim is not established. Tables 4 and 11 add the Macro-Encoder and DGCL together, confounding temporal capacity with the proposed objective. Age/sex prediction and demographic clustering mainly verify recovery of pretraining supervision; they do not establish learning of sleep cycles. Temporal-shuffling controls, an order-invariant pooling baseline, and comparisons with direct demographic prediction or another temporal pretraining objective are missing. Similarly, the claimed explanation for segmentation gains lacks a segmentation-specific MAE/CL ablation.

Disease-prediction evidence is insufficiently specified. The manuscript omits outcome-specific event counts, follow-up distributions, prevalent-disease exclusions, and detailed censoring rules. Table 10 lists a Cox-loss batch size of four subjects without explaining how population risk sets are constructed or approximated. Crucially, there is no demographic-only baseline or test of incremental value beyond age, sex, and BMI, despite these being explicit pretraining targets and relevant disease predictors. The reported concordance therefore does not establish added clinical value from sleep architecture.

Evaluation does not support the broad superiority and generalization claims. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run results, including for few-shot experiments whose results can depend strongly on selected subjects. MOMENT substantially outperforms SleepMaMi on KISS staging (69.8 versus 62.8 accuracy), and disease results are mixed. Most evaluations use cohorts represented during pretraining; the unseen ISRUC experiment compares only against SleepFM. Baseline feature extraction, temporal context, and tuning are insufficiently documented to establish comparability.

Reproducibility and reporting require corrections. No code/checkpoint availability statement is provided, and important representation pooling and downstream readout details remain unclear. Section 3.3 describes resampling to 100 Hz followed by filtering up to 60 Hz and a 60 Hz notch, which requires clarification relative to the 50 Hz Nyquist limit. Table 9 calls 60 seconds '120 epochs,' inconsistent with the 30-second epoch definition. Figure 11's SHHS1 staging confusion matrix yields pooled kappa approximately 0.743, whereas Table 1 reports 0.700; a different aggregation protocol, if used, should be explained.

Limitations and research ethics: The hardware-shift discussion is welcome, and Appendix A.4 documents IRB approval and de-identification for KVSS. However, demographic supervision warrants analysis of performance across age, sex, and BMI groups and discussion of demographic shortcuts. Calling metadata 'noise-free ground truth' for macro-structure is unjustified: demographic similarity does not imply similar individual sleep architecture. Claims of reliable clinical application exceed the presented discrimination metrics and limited external validation.

strengths: Significance: Integrating second-scale PSG features with full-night context addresses a useful clinical representation-learning problem. Evaluation spans sleep staging, breathing-event segmentation, disease prediction, and limited-label adaptation, including cohorts excluded from pretraining.

Originality: The combination of private/shared micro-encoders and a bidirectional macro-encoder trained through demographic-weighted contrastive learning constitutes a coherent methodological contribution, although its components build on established methods.

Soundness: The appendix provides substantial ablations, including reconstruction versus contrastive learning, demographic factors, temporal intervals, macro-encoder architectures, and alternative pretraining objectives. Including LSTM downstream heads and task-specialized baselines usefully broadens the evaluation.

Presentation and reproducibility: Architecture diagrams, dataset descriptions, channel specifications, and hyperparameter tables make much of the pipeline understandable. The manuscript acknowledges demographic-bias risks and the empirical nature of its demographic distance function.
weaknesses: Soundness—unresolved subject overlap: Appendix A.2 states that all SHHS2 recordings enter pretraining while SHHS1 is partitioned for downstream evaluation. SHHS2 is a follow-up visit of SHHS participants, but no exclusion of SHHS1 validation/test participants from SHHS2 pretraining is described. Consequently, subject-independent evaluation is not established, including for the central SHHS disease-prediction results. Participant-level deduplication across visits and reevaluation are needed.

Soundness—contradictory numerical evidence: Figure 11's KISS staging confusion matrix yields approximately 62.8% accuracy and 60.6% macro-F1, rather than Table 1's 71.0% and 70.0%. Its KISS SDB matrix yields approximately 81.8% accuracy and 75.4% macro-F1, rather than Table 2's 85.5% and 78.0%. The SHHS staging matrix gives approximately 74.3% kappa, versus 70.0% in Table 1. Different aggregation or evaluation protocols could explain some differences, but none are identified; these discrepancies require reconciliation.

Soundness and originality—the central DGCL interpretation is insufficiently demonstrated: Demographic clustering and improved demographic prediction establish that representations encode the training targets, not that they recover temporal sleep architecture. Table 16 shows only 0.1–0.2 percentage-point accuracy advantages over SimCLR/DINO, without uncertainty estimates. Temporal-order controls, direct macrostructure measurements, and demographic-only or demographic-adjusted clinical baselines would help distinguish temporal learning from demographic correlates.

Evaluation uncertainty: No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are supplied for the principal comparisons, few-shot experiments, or subgroup analyses. This particularly limits conclusions about the small DGCL gains and disease-prediction differences. The disease evaluation also omits event counts, detailed outcome eligibility and censoring information, and calibration, leaving claims of reliable clinical application premature.

Reproducibility: The CFS/SOF downstream partition and probe-training protocols are insufficiently specified. In particular, Table 6 lists 669 CFS subjects overall, while Section 4.2 describes 669 training samples plus a test split. The manuscript's code/checkpoint availability sentence contains no link. Preprocessing also requires clarification: Section 3.3 describes resampling to 100 Hz before a 60 Hz ECG cutoff and 60 Hz notch filtering, which cannot be implemented as stated after resampling.

Significance and presentation: Broad superiority claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Several contemporary sleep foundation models discussed in related work are not evaluated. Under the LSTM protocol, some advantages become modest, and specialized models outperform SleepMaMi; notably, Table 19 reports SDB macro-F1 of 74.6 for AIX versus 60.6 for SleepMaMi. These results support a potentially useful transferable representation, but not unqualified state-of-the-art clinical performance.

Research ethics: Recognizing demographic-bias risks is appropriate, but Appendix E's assertion that DGCL does not introduce or amplify bias is unsupported by coarse subgroup-average C-indices without uncertainty, calibration, or intersectional analysis. Physiological inputs can encode demographic proxies even when metadata are absent at inference. Table 11 also shows a larger sex performance gap for SleepMaMi than for Micro-only. The fairness conclusion should be narrowed to the evidence.

strengths: Significance: Integrating second-scale PSG features with full-night context addresses a useful clinical representation-learning problem. Evaluation spans sleep staging, breathing-event segmentation, disease prediction, and limited-label adaptation, including cohorts excluded from pretraining.

Empirical merits: The reported foundation-model comparisons show substantial improvements, particularly for SDB segmentation on CFS and SOF (Table 2). The LSTM-head evaluation also reports gains over SleepFM across all six disease outcomes (Table 18).

Originality: The combination of private/shared multimodal encoding and demographic-guided full-night pretraining is a plausible methodological contribution. The appendix includes relevant comparisons against alternative architectures, demographic objectives, and SimCLR/DINO pretraining.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architectural motivation and diagrams are clear, and Appendices A–C provide substantial dataset, architecture, and optimization details. Including specialized-model comparisons and demographic subgroup analyses improves the evaluation's breadth.
weaknesses: Soundness—possible participant leakage: Appendix A.2 states that SHHS1 is split for downstream evaluation while the entire SHHS2 dataset is used for pretraining. SHHS2 contains follow-up visits from SHHS participants, but no exclusion of SHHS1 validation/test participants is documented. This leaves a serious risk of participant overlap and, for prospective disease prediction, exposure to later physiological recordings. A participant-level overlap audit and evaluation with all visits of held-out individuals excluded are necessary.

Soundness—internally inconsistent results: Recalculating metrics from Figure 11 gives KISS sleep-staging accuracy/Macro-F1 of approximately 62.8/60.6, versus 71.0/70.0 in Table 1. The KISS SDB matrix gives approximately 81.8/75.4, versus 85.5/78.0 in Table 2. The SHHS staging matrix agrees with the reported accuracy and Macro-F1 but implies kappa approximately 74.3 rather than 70.0. These discrepancies require an explanation of any differing protocols or aggregation and corrected, auditable results.

Soundness and originality—the central DGCL interpretation is insufficiently established: Demographic clustering demonstrates recovery of its supervisory attributes, not necessarily learning of sleep cycles or temporal architecture. Table 16 reports only 0.1–0.2 percentage-point accuracy improvements over SimCLR/DINO, without uncertainty estimates. Temporal-order controls, direct macrostructure evaluation, and demographic-only or demographic-adjusted disease baselines are needed to establish what DGCL contributes beyond demographic risk encoding and generic sequence modeling.

Clinical evidence is incomplete: Disease prediction is evaluated only on SHHS1, without reporting endpoint-specific event counts, censoring distributions, prevalent-disease exclusions, confidence intervals, or calibration. The definition and construction of survival risk sets also need clarification given the four-subject training batches in Table 10. Consequently, the claims of reliable clinical applicability exceed the evidence.

Significance and comparison scope: Gains are strongest under linear probing and narrow considerably with LSTM heads (Table 17). Specialized models outperform SleepMaMi on staging, and AIX obtains 74.6 SDB Macro-F1 versus 60.6 for SleepMaMi (Table 19). These results do not negate the value of a reusable representation, but they limit claims of broad superiority. The absence of repeated runs, few-shot sampling variability, and detailed baseline tuning protocols further weakens comparative conclusions.

Reproducibility and presentation: The statement that source code and checkpoints are available ends without a link. Important implementation details remain ambiguous, including downstream feature pooling/alignment and exact participant splits. The preprocessing description resamples to 100 Hz before specifying a 60 Hz ECG cutoff and notch filter, which requires clarification because those frequencies exceed the resulting Nyquist limit.

Ethics and limitations: Acknowledging demographic bias is appropriate, but Appendix E overstates what its analysis establishes. Demographics can act as shortcuts through physiological representations even when absent from model inputs. Average subgroup C-indices without uncertainty, calibration, or intersectional analysis cannot confirm that DGCL does not introduce or amplify bias; the reported sex performance gap actually increases relative to Micro-only. Fairness and equitable-deployment claims should be qualified.

strengths: Significance: Integrating second-scale physiological features with full-night context addresses a useful problem in sleep analysis. Pretraining on 20,964 recordings across multiple cohorts and evaluating staging, breathing-event segmentation, and disease prediction gives the contribution substantial practical scope.

Methodology: The private/shared Micro-Encoder and bidirectional Mamba Macro-Encoder form a coherent architecture. Appendix F includes useful component, architecture, demographic-factor, and pretraining-objective ablations, plus comparisons using LSTM downstream heads.

Empirical merits: Tables 1–2 report substantial improvements over the evaluated foundation models, particularly for breathing-event Macro-F1. Evaluation on cohorts excluded from pretraining and the few-shot experiments provide encouraging evidence for transferable representations.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main architecture and objectives are generally understandable, with informative diagrams and detailed architecture and hyperparameter tables. The manuscript also acknowledges demographic-bias risks and provides an initial subgroup analysis.
weaknesses: Soundness—material inconsistencies in reported results: The KISS staging confusion matrix in Figure 11 implies 62.8% accuracy and 60.6% Macro-F1, whereas Table 1 reports 71.0% and 70.0%. The KISS breathing-event matrix implies 81.8% accuracy and 75.4% Macro-F1, versus 85.5% and 78.0% in Table 2. The SHHS staging matrix reproduces the reported accuracy and Macro-F1 but implies kappa approximately 0.743, versus 0.700 in Table 1. Different aggregation or evaluation protocols could explain some discrepancies, but none is specified. These results need reconciliation before the headline improvements can be trusted.

Soundness—participant separation is unresolved: Appendix A.2 explicitly uses the entire SHHS2 dataset for pretraining while holding out SHHS1 participants for evaluation. SHHS2 is a follow-up visit of the same cohort, and the manuscript does not document exclusion of SHHS1 validation/test participants from SHHS2 pretraining. Consequently, participant-independent evaluation is not established; later recordings could also compromise the prospective interpretation of disease prediction. Participant-level deduplication across visits and a clean reevaluation are necessary.

Soundness—the central macrostructure interpretation is insufficiently established: DGCL directly encourages demographic encoding, and the demographic UMAPs primarily verify that objective. They do not show that the model learns sleep architecture beyond demographic or cohort correlates. Table 16 reports only 0.1–0.2 percentage-point accuracy gains over SimCLR/DINO, without uncertainty. Temporal-order perturbations, direct sleep-architecture measurements, and demographic-only or demographic-adjusted disease baselines would help distinguish temporal understanding from demographic proxy learning.

Evaluation and statistical support: Results lack confidence intervals, repeated-seed variability, and repeated few-shot subject selections. This is particularly consequential for the small DGCL improvements and disease comparisons. Disease evaluation also omits essential information about event counts, follow-up, censoring, prevalent-disease exclusions, and endpoint selection. Table 10 specifies a disease-training batch size of four subjects without explaining how Cox risk sets in Equation 7 are computed.

Originality and significance are overstated: The integration is potentially useful, but its components largely combine established techniques, and the strongest claims of being the first or universal model are not adequately differentiated from the recent sleep foundation models discussed in Section 2. SleepGPT, Sleep2Vec, and OSF are not evaluated. Appendix comparisons also qualify the broad performance claims: on SHHS, specialized staging models outperform SleepMaMi, and AIX achieves 74.6% breathing-event Macro-F1 versus 60.6%. These results do not negate the value of a reusable representation, but they warrant narrower claims.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: The source-code/checkpoint availability sentence ends without a link. Exact external-cohort splits, baseline adaptation details, downstream feature pooling, and several implementation choices are insufficiently specified. The preprocessing description also needs clarification: after stating that signals are resampled to 100 Hz, it specifies a 60 Hz ECG cutoff and 60 Hz notch filter, which cannot be implemented conventionally at that sampling rate.

Ethics and limitations: The acknowledgement of demographic bias is appropriate, but Appendix E overclaims that subgroup results confirm DGCL does not introduce or amplify bias. Demographics need not be explicit inputs for a model to learn demographic proxies. Averaged C-indices without subgroup sample sizes, uncertainty, calibration, or intersectional analyses cannot establish fairness; Table 11 also shows a larger sex performance gap than the Micro-only model. Claims of equitable or reliable clinical application should be tempered.
